stem: When a number of droplets coalesce to form a single drop, the total surface area of the drop _____.
solution:
**(A)** decreases

Let \(n\) droplets each of radius \(r\) merge into one drop of radius \(R\). Volume is conserved:

\(n \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\), so \(R = n^{1/3}r\)

Total area before merging \(= n \times 4\pi r^{2}\)

Area after merging \(= 4\pi R^{2} = 4\pi n^{2/3}r^{2}\)

Since \(n^{2/3} < n\) for \(n > 1\), the final area is smaller.

\(\therefore\) the total surface area decreases. The surface energy released in this way is what makes small drops coalesce spontaneously and warms the resulting drop slightly.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Behaviour of Gases, Ideal and Real Gas
stem: In an ideal gas, molecules possess _____.

options.label: B
options.text: both kinetic energy and potential energy

options.label: D
options.text: neither kinetic energy nor potential energy

solution:
**(A)** only kinetic energy

An ideal gas is defined by the assumption that its molecules exert no force on one another except during the instant of an elastic collision. Potential energy requires a force acting over a distance between molecules, and in an ideal gas there is none.

The molecules are in continuous random motion, so they do have kinetic energy.

\(\therefore\) the molecules possess only kinetic energy, which is why the internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: If the frequency of incident radiation is increased above threshold frequency, keeping intensity and potential constant then the photoelectric current _____.
solution:
**(C)** remains same

The photoelectric current is decided by the number of photoelectrons reaching the anode per second, and that in turn is decided by the number of photons striking the metal per second, which is the intensity.

Raising the frequency above the threshold gives each emitted electron a larger maximum kinetic energy, through \(K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0\), but it does not change how many electrons are emitted while the intensity is held constant. With the collecting potential also held constant, the saturation current is unaltered.

\(\therefore\) the photoelectric current remains the same. Frequency controls the energy of the photoelectrons; intensity controls their number.

stem: The process in which heat is neither absorbed nor released by a system is called _____.
solution:
**(D)** adiabatic

An adiabatic process is by definition one in which no heat enters or leaves the system, \(Q = 0\). It is achieved by insulating the system perfectly, or by carrying out the change so quickly that there is no time for heat exchange.

\(\therefore\) the process is adiabatic. Of the others, an isobaric process holds pressure constant, an isochoric process holds volume constant and an isothermal process holds temperature constant, and all three exchange heat with the surroundings.

stem: The period of conical pendulum in terms of its length \((l)\), semi-vertical angle \((\theta)\) and acceleration due to gravity \((g)\) is _____.
solution:
**(C)** \(4\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l\cos\theta}{4g}}\)

For a conical pendulum of string length \(l\) making a semi-vertical angle \(\theta\), the standard result for the period is

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l\cos\theta}{g}}\)

That exact form is not printed, but option (c) is the same expression written differently. Taking the 4 out of the denominator of the radical,

\(4\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l\cos\theta}{4g}} = 4\pi \times \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{l\cos\theta}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l\cos\theta}{g}}\)

\(\therefore\) option (c) is the period. Note that \(l\cos\theta\) is the vertical height of the apex above the plane of the circle, so a conical pendulum has the period of a simple pendulum of that height.

stem: A conducting rod of length \(l\), rotates about one of its ends in a uniform magnetic field \(B\), with a constant angular velocity \(\omega\). If the plane of rotation is perpendicular to \(B\), the e.m.f. induced between the ends of rod is _____.
solution:
**(A)** \(\dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)

The rod is pivoted at one end, so different elements move with different speeds. Take an element of length \(dx\) at distance \(x\) from the pivot. Its speed is \(v = \omega x\), and the emf induced across it is

\(de = B v\,dx = B\omega x\,dx\)

The whole rod is a series chain of such elements, so the emfs add:

\(e = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{l} B\omega x\,dx = B\omega\left[\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{l}\)

\(\therefore e = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega l^{2}\)

The factor of one half appears because the rod's average speed is half its tip speed. Option (b) is the result of using the tip speed for the whole rod.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: A metal surface is illuminated by photons of energy 5 eV and 2.5 eV respectively. The ratio of their wavelengths of emitted radiation is _____.
solution:
**(B)** 1 : 2

The energy of a photon and its wavelength are related by

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\), so \(\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{E}\)

Taking the ratio for the two photons,

\(\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{E_2}{E_1} = \dfrac{2.5}{5} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the wavelengths are in the ratio \(1 : 2\). The more energetic photon has the shorter wavelength.

stem: A particle is subjected to two parallel S.H.M.s such that \(x = 2\sin\omega t\) and \(y = 2\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\). The amplitude of the resultant S.H.M. will be _____.
solution:
**(B)** \(2\sqrt{3}\)

For two parallel S.H.M.s of amplitudes \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) with a phase difference \(\delta\), the resultant amplitude is

\(A = \sqrt{a_1^{2} + a_2^{2} + 2a_1a_2\cos\delta}\)

Here \(a_1 = a_2 = 2\) and \(\delta = \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 60^{\circ}\), so \(\cos\delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(A = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 2(2)(2)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\)

\(A = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 4} = \sqrt{12}\)

\(\therefore A = 2\sqrt{3}\)

Option (d), 12, is the value of \(A^{2}\), offered for a student who stops before taking the square root.

stem: A bar magnet of magnetic moment \(10\ \text{Am}^{2}\) has a cross-sectional area of \(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2}\). If the intensity of magnetisation of magnet is \(10^{6}\) A/m, the length of the bar magnet is _____.
solution:
**(B)** 4 cm

The intensity of magnetisation is the magnetic moment per unit volume:

\(M_z = \dfrac{M}{V}\), so \(V = \dfrac{M}{M_z}\)

\(V = \dfrac{10}{10^{6}} = 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^{3}\)

For a bar magnet of uniform cross-section, \(V = A \times L\), so

\(L = \dfrac{V}{A} = \dfrac{10^{-5}}{2.5 \times 10^{-4}}\)

\(L = 0.04\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore\) the length of the bar magnet is \(0.04\ \text{m}\), that is \(4\ \text{cm}\).

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: In series LCR circuit for \(X_L > X_C\), \(\tan\phi\) will be _____.
solution:
**(C)** positive

In a series LCR circuit the phase angle between the applied voltage and the current is given by

\(\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}\)

The resistance \(R\) is always positive. When \(X_L > X_C\) the numerator is positive as well.

\(\therefore \tan\phi\) is positive. The circuit is inductive, the current lags behind the voltage, and \(\phi\) lies between \(0\) and \(90^{\circ}\).

stem: State the formula for electric field intensity due to uniformly charged spherical shell.
solution:
For a uniformly charged spherical shell of radius \(R\) carrying total charge \(q\), the electric field intensity at a point distant \(r\) from its centre is

**Outside the shell** \((r > R)\):

\(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^{2}}\)

The shell behaves as though its whole charge were concentrated at its centre.

**Inside the shell** \((r < R)\):

\(E = 0\)

since a Gaussian surface drawn inside encloses no charge.

stem: Name an instrument for measurement of e.m.f. of a cell.
solution:
A **potentiometer** is used to measure the e.m.f. of a cell.

It is preferred to a voltmeter because at the balance point it draws **no current** from the cell, so the cell's internal resistance causes no potential drop and the reading is the true e.m.f. rather than the terminal voltage. A voltmeter always draws some current and therefore reads slightly low.

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
stem: Calculate the magnitude of force experienced by a stationary charge exposed to uniform magnetic field.
solution:
The force experienced by a charge moving in a magnetic field is

\(F = qvB\sin\theta\)

For a stationary charge the speed is zero, so \(v = 0\), and the whole product vanishes whatever the values of \(q\), \(B\) and \(\theta\).

\(F = q(0)B\sin\theta = 0\)

\(\therefore F = 0\)

A magnetic field exerts a force only on a moving charge. A charge at rest in a uniform magnetic field experiences no force at all, which is one of the ways a magnetic field differs from an electric field.

subtopic: Permanent Magnets, Electromagnets and Magnetic Shielding
stem: Which property of bar magnet is used in navigation?
solution:
The **directive property** of a bar magnet is used in navigation.

A bar magnet suspended freely so that it can turn in a horizontal plane always comes to rest pointing approximately north and south, because the earth's magnetic field exerts a couple on it until its magnetic moment lines up with the field. This is the principle of the mariner's compass.

subtopic: Interference and Young's Double Slit Experiment
stem: In Young's double slit experiment, width of the two slits are in the ratio 25 : 1. Calculate the ratio of amplitudes.
solution:
In Young's experiment the intensity passing through a slit is proportional to its width, and the amplitude is proportional to the square root of the intensity:

\(\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{w_1}{w_2} = \dfrac{25}{1}\)

\(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{25}{1}}\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{5}{1}\), so the amplitudes are in the ratio \(5 : 1\).

stem: What is beta plus decay?
solution:
**Beta plus decay** is a radioactive decay in which a proton inside the nucleus changes into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino:

\(p \rightarrow n + e^{+} + \nu\)

The nuclear reaction is

\(^{A}_{Z}X \rightarrow\ ^{A}_{Z-1}Y + e^{+} + \nu\)

The mass number stays the same while the atomic number falls by one, so the daughter nucleus is the element one place earlier in the periodic table. It occurs in nuclei having too many protons for stability.

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: If the tension in sonometer wire is increased by 21%, compare the initial frequency with the later.
solution:
For a stretched wire the fundamental frequency varies as the square root of the tension:

\(n \propto \sqrt{T}\), so \(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}\)

The tension is increased by 21 per cent, so \(T_2 = 1.21\,T_1\).

\(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \sqrt{1.21} = 1.1\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{1}{1.1} = \dfrac{10}{11}\)

The initial and final frequencies are in the ratio \(10 : 11\), so the frequency rises by 10 per cent.

stem: Define second's pendulum.
solution:
A **second's pendulum** is a simple pendulum whose period is exactly **two seconds**, so that each swing from one extreme to the other takes one second.

From \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\) with \(T = 2\ \text{s}\), its length is

\(L = \dfrac{gT^{2}}{4\pi^{2}} = \dfrac{g}{\pi^{2}}\)

which is about \(0.993\ \text{m}\) at a place where \(g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^{2}\). Since \(g\) varies from place to place, so does the length of a second's pendulum.

stem: What are Eddy currents? State its two applications.
solution:
**Eddy currents.** When the magnetic flux through the body of a solid conductor changes, induced currents are set up in the body of the conductor itself. Because the conductor offers a continuous medium, these currents flow in closed loops, circulating like eddies in water, and are called eddy currents or Foucault currents. Their direction obeys Lenz's law, so they always oppose the change producing them, and the energy they carry appears as heat in the conductor.

**Two applications:**

**1. Electromagnetic braking.** A metal disc attached to the wheels of a train is made to rotate between the poles of a strong electromagnet. Eddy currents induced in the disc oppose its motion and bring the train smoothly to rest, with no mechanical contact and so no wear.

**2. Induction furnace.** A metal charge placed in a coil carrying a high frequency alternating current develops very large eddy currents, and the heat they produce melts the metal. This is used to prepare alloys in a vacuum.

stem: State any two sources of error in meter bridge experiment. Explain how they can be minimised.
solution:
**Two sources of error and how they are minimised:**

**1. Contact resistance and resistance of the thick copper strips.** The end points of the metre bridge wire, the copper strips and the connecting terminals all have a small resistance of their own, which is not included in the two arms but adds to them. This end error shifts the null point away from its true position.

It is minimised by **interchanging the known and unknown resistances** in the two gaps and repeating the observation. The end error affects the two readings oppositely, so the mean of the two values of the unknown resistance is nearly free of it.

**2. Non-uniform cross-section of the bridge wire.** The balance condition assumes that resistance is proportional to length, which is true only if the wire is uniform. Any variation in thickness makes the lengths an unfaithful measure of the resistances.

It is minimised by taking readings with the **null point near the middle** of the wire, where the fractional error is least, and by **repeating the experiment after interchanging the ends** so that errors from either half tend to cancel.

A third precaution is to pass current only while taking a reading, so that heating does not change the resistance of the wire.

subtopic: Interference and Young's Double Slit Experiment
stem: Draw a ray diagram showing position of virtual sources and region of interference in biprism experiment.
solution:
**Ray diagram of the biprism experiment.**

A biprism is a single prism of very small refracting angle, of the order of half a degree, with its base broad; it behaves as two thin prisms placed base to base.

Light from a narrow monochromatic slit S falls on the biprism. The upper half of the beam is refracted downward by the upper prism, and the lower half is refracted upward by the lower prism. To an eye receiving these two beams, they appear to diverge from two virtual images of the slit, \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), lying in the plane of S and very close together.

Because \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are both images of one slit, they are **coherent**, and this is the purpose of the biprism.

The two refracted beams overlap in the shaded region beyond the biprism, and interference fringes are formed everywhere in that region, which is why the pattern can be picked up at any distance beyond it. The eyepiece placed in this region shows equally spaced bright and dark bands.

In the diagram, S is the slit, the biprism stands with its base vertical a short distance away, \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) are marked just above and below S, and the overlapping region of the two emergent beams is shaded as the region of interference.

stem: Derive an expression for radius of \(n^{\text{th}}\) Bohr orbit.
solution:
Consider a hydrogen-like atom of atomic number \(Z\), with an electron of mass \(m\) and charge \(e\) moving in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) with speed \(v\).

**The electrostatic force provides the centripetal force:**

\(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)

\(mv^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{r}\)   ... (1)

**Bohr's quantisation condition:**

\(mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}\), so \(v = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}\)   ... (2)

Substituting (2) into (1),

\(m\left(\dfrac{nh}{2\pi mr}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Ze^{2}}{r}\)

\(\dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}mr^{2}} = \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\)

Cancelling one power of \(r\) and rearranging,

\(\therefore r_n = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 n^{2}h^{2}}{\pi m Z e^{2}}\)

The radius is proportional to \(n^{2}\), so the allowed orbits are not equally spaced but get rapidly farther apart. For hydrogen, \(Z = 1\) and \(n = 1\), the radius is \(0.53\ \text{Å}\), called the Bohr radius.

stem: A ceiling fan has moment of inertia of \(2\ \text{kg m}^{2}\). It attains maximum frequency of 60 r.p.m. in \(2\pi\) seconds. Calculate its power rating.
solution:
The fan reaches a frequency of 60 r.p.m., that is 1 revolution per second, so its final angular speed is

\(\omega = 2\pi n = 2\pi\ \text{rad/s}\)

Starting from rest and taking \(2\pi\) seconds to reach it, the angular acceleration is

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\omega - \omega_0}{t} = \dfrac{2\pi - 0}{2\pi} = 1\ \text{rad/s}^{2}\)

The torque is

\(\tau = I\alpha = 2 \times 1 = 2\ \text{N m}\)

The power rating is the power developed at the working speed:

\(P = \tau\omega = 2 \times 2\pi\)

\(P = 4\pi = 12.57\ \text{W}\)

\(\therefore\) the power rating of the ceiling fan is about \(12.57\ \text{W}\).

subtopic: Potential Energy of Charges and Dipoles
stem: An electric dipole consists of two unlike charges of magnitude \(2 \times 10^{-6}\) C each and separated by 4 cm. The dipole is placed in an external electric field of \(10^{5}\) N/C. Calculate the work done by an external agent to turn the dipole through 180°.
solution:
The dipole moment is

\(p = q \times 2l = 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{-2}\)

\(p = 8 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{C m}\)

The potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field at angle \(\theta\) to the field is \(U = -pE\cos\theta\). Turning it through \(180^{\circ}\), from \(\theta = 0\) to \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\), the work done by the external agent is

\(W = U_{180} - U_{0} = (+pE) - (-pE) = 2pE\)

Substituting \(E = 10^{5}\ \text{N/C}\),

\(W = 2 \times 8 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{5}\)

\(W = 1.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{J}\)

\(\therefore\) the work done in turning the dipole through \(180^{\circ}\) is \(0.016\ \text{J}\).

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current
stem: Derive an expression for the magnetic field produced by a current in a circular arc of a wire using Biot-Savart law.
solution:
By the Biot-Savart law, a current element \(I\,\overrightarrow{dl}\) produces at a point distant \(r\) a magnetic induction

\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^{2}}\)

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the element and the line joining it to the point.

Consider a circular arc of radius \(r\) subtending an angle \(\phi\) at the centre, and take the point to be the centre itself. For every element of the arc, the radius is perpendicular to the element, so \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\) and \(\sin\theta = 1\). Also every element is at the same distance \(r\).

\(dB = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl}{r^{2}}\)

Every element contributes a field in the same direction, perpendicular to the plane of the arc, so the magnitudes add directly:

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r^{2}}\displaystyle\int dl = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r^{2}} \times (\text{length of arc})\)

The length of an arc subtending \(\phi\) at the centre is \(r\phi\), so

\(\therefore B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I\phi}{4\pi r}\)

For a complete circular loop, \(\phi = 2\pi\) and this reduces to \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}\).

stem: State advantages and disadvantages of photodiode.
solution:
**Advantages of a photodiode:**

1. Its response to a change in light intensity is extremely quick, so it is suitable for high speed detection and for optical communication.
2. It is small, light and mechanically rugged, and it needs a low operating voltage.
3. Its output current varies linearly with the incident light intensity over a wide range, which makes it convenient for measurement.
4. It has a long working life and is inexpensive to manufacture.

**Disadvantages of a photodiode:**

1. It passes a small **dark current** even when no light falls on it, which sets a limit on the weakest signal it can detect.
2. Its performance depends strongly on **temperature**, since the dark current rises as the temperature rises.
3. The active area is small, so the light has to be focused on it.
4. Its sensitivity is low compared with a photomultiplier tube.

stem:
Distinguish between harmonics and overtones.
[Any Two points]
solution:
| Harmonics | Overtones |
|---|---|
| A harmonic is any integral multiple of the fundamental frequency, whether or not that frequency is actually produced by the body. | An overtone is a frequency higher than the fundamental that the body **actually** produces. |
| They are counted from the fundamental itself, which is the first harmonic. | They are counted after the fundamental, so the first overtone is the next frequency the body emits above it. |
| The set of harmonics is fixed by the fundamental alone: \(n, 2n, 3n, \ldots\) | Which overtones occur depends on the body and the way it vibrates, so a pipe closed at one end has only the odd harmonics as its overtones. |

For a pipe closed at one end, for example, the first overtone is the third harmonic, since the even harmonics are not produced at all.

stem:
A steel ball with radius 0.3 mm is falling with velocity of 2 m/s through a tube filled with glycerine. Calculate viscous force acting on the steel ball.
[ Given : \(\eta_{glycerine} = 0.833\ Ns/m^{2}\) ]
solution:
For a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid, the viscous force is given by Stokes' law:

\(F = 6\pi\eta r v\)

Here \(\eta = 0.833\ Ns/m^{2}\), \(r = 0.3\ \text{mm} = 0.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}\) and \(v = 2\ \text{m/s}\).

\(F = 6 \times 3.142 \times 0.833 \times 0.3 \times 10^{-3} \times 2\)

\(F = 18.852 \times 0.833 \times 0.6 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(F = 15.70 \times 0.6 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(F = 9.42 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}\)

\(\therefore\) the viscous force acting on the steel ball is \(9.42 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}\).

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: RMS Speed and Interpretation of Temperature
stem:
Calculate the temperature at which the average kinetic energy of a molecule of a gas will be same as that of an electron accelerated through 1 volt.
[ Given: \(k_B = 1.4 \times 10^{-23}\) J/k, \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\)C ]
solution:
The average kinetic energy of a gas molecule at absolute temperature \(T\) is

\(\overline{KE} = \dfrac{3}{2}k_BT\)

An electron accelerated through a potential difference \(V\) gains kinetic energy

\(KE = eV = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1 = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\)

Equating the two,

\(\dfrac{3}{2}k_BT = eV\)

\(T = \dfrac{2eV}{3k_B} = \dfrac{2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{3 \times 1.4 \times 10^{-23}}\)

\(T = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-19}}{4.2 \times 10^{-23}}\)

\(T = 7619\ \text{K}\)

\(\therefore\) the required temperature is about \(7.62 \times 10^{3}\ \text{K}\).

subtopic: Phasors and Types of AC Circuits
stem: An inductor of inductance 200 mH is connected to an A.C. source of peak e.m.f. 220 V and frequency 50 Hz. Calculate the peak current in the circuit.
solution:
For a pure inductor the opposition to alternating current is the inductive reactance

\(X_L = 2\pi n L\)

Here \(n = 50\ \text{Hz}\) and \(L = 200\ \text{mH} = 0.2\ \text{H}\).

\(X_L = 2 \times 3.142 \times 50 \times 0.2\)

\(X_L = 62.84\ \Omega\)

The peak current follows from the peak emf:

\(i_0 = \dfrac{e_0}{X_L} = \dfrac{220}{62.84}\)

\(i_0 = 3.50\ \text{A}\)

\(\therefore\) the peak current in the circuit is about \(3.5\ \text{A}\).

subtopic: Thermodynamic State Variables and the p-V Diagram
stem:
In thermodynamics, define :
(a) Mechanical equilibrium
(b) Chemical equilibrium
(c) Thermal equilibrium
solution:
**(a) Mechanical equilibrium.** A system is in mechanical equilibrium when there is no unbalanced force anywhere within it, and none between it and its surroundings. The pressure is then uniform throughout the system and equal to that of the surroundings, so no part of it accelerates and its volume does not change.

**(b) Chemical equilibrium.** A system is in chemical equilibrium when its chemical composition does not change with time. There is no net chemical reaction going on and no net diffusion of matter from one part of the system to another or across its boundary.

**(c) Thermal equilibrium.** A system is in thermal equilibrium when its temperature is the same at every point within it and equal to that of the surroundings. There is then no net flow of heat within the system or between it and the surroundings.

A system in all three at once is said to be in thermodynamic equilibrium, and only then can a single set of state variables describe it.

stem: Derive an expression for resonant frequency of series resonant circuit.
solution:
In a series LCR circuit connected to an alternating source, the impedance is

\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}}\)

The current \(I_{rms} = \dfrac{e_{rms}}{Z}\) is greatest when \(Z\) is least, and \(Z\) is least when the reactive term vanishes. This condition is called **series resonance**:

\(X_L = X_C\)

Substituting the expressions for the two reactances,

\(\omega_r L = \dfrac{1}{\omega_r C}\)

\(\omega_r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{LC}\)

\(\omega_r = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\)

Writing \(\omega_r = 2\pi n_r\),

\(\therefore n_r = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}\)

At this frequency \(Z = R\), the current is maximum and in phase with the applied voltage, and the circuit is purely resistive. The resonant frequency depends only on \(L\) and \(C\), not on \(R\).

subtopic: Angular S.H.M. and Magnet Vibrating in a Magnetic Field
stem: Obtain an expression for period of a bar magnet vibrating in a uniform magnetic field and performing angular S.H.M.
solution:
Consider a bar magnet of magnetic moment \(M\) and moment of inertia \(I\), suspended so that it can turn freely in a horizontal uniform magnetic field of induction \(B\).

When the magnet is displaced through a small angle \(\theta\) from the field direction, the field exerts on it a restoring couple

\(\tau = -MB\sin\theta\)

the minus sign showing that the couple acts so as to reduce \(\theta\). For small angular displacements, \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) in radian, so

\(\tau = -MB\theta\)

The couple is proportional to the angular displacement and oppositely directed, which is the condition for angular S.H.M.

Writing \(\tau = I\alpha\),

\(I\dfrac{d^{2}\theta}{dt^{2}} = -MB\theta\)

\(\dfrac{d^{2}\theta}{dt^{2}} = -\left(\dfrac{MB}{I}\right)\theta\)

Comparing with \(\dfrac{d^{2}\theta}{dt^{2}} = -\omega^{2}\theta\),

\(\omega^{2} = \dfrac{MB}{I}\)

The period is \(T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\), so

\(\therefore T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{MB}}\)

This relation is the basis of the vibration magnetometer, which compares magnetic moments or field strengths by timing such oscillations.

stem: Define magnetization. State its S.I. unit and dimensions. What is the relation between permeability and magnetic susceptibility?
solution:
**Magnetization.** The magnetization of a material is the net magnetic moment per unit volume of the material:

\(M_z = \dfrac{M_{net}}{V}\)

It measures the extent to which the material has become magnetised, that is, how far the atomic magnetic moments within it have been aligned.

**S.I. unit:** ampere per metre, \(\text{A/m}\), since it is \(\dfrac{\text{A m}^{2}}{\text{m}^{3}}\).

**Dimensions:** \([M^{0}L^{-1}T^{0}I^{1}]\).

**Relation between permeability and susceptibility.** Inside a magnetised material the total field is the sum of the applied field and the field due to the magnetization:

\(B = \mu_0(H + M_z)\)

Since \(M_z = \chi H\), where \(\chi\) is the magnetic susceptibility,

\(B = \mu_0 H(1 + \chi)\)

But \(B = \mu H\), where \(\mu\) is the permeability of the material, so

\(\mu = \mu_0(1 + \chi)\)

\(\therefore \mu_r = \dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0} = 1 + \chi\)

The relative permeability exceeds one by exactly the susceptibility.

stem: Derive an expression for electric potential due to a point charge.
solution:
Let a point charge \(+q\) be placed at the origin O. The electric potential at a point P distant \(r\) from O is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to P against the field.

At a distance \(x\) from the charge the field is

\(E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{x^{2}}\)

directed outward. To move a unit positive test charge inward through \(dx\) against this field, the external agent does work \(dW = -E\,dx\), the minus sign appearing because the displacement is opposite to the field.

The total work in bringing it from infinity to P is

\(V = -\displaystyle\int_{\infty}^{r} E\,dx = -\int_{\infty}^{r}\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{x^{2}}\,dx\)

\(V = -\dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{\infty}^{r}\)

\(V = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\dfrac{1}{r} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right]\)

\(\therefore V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r}\)

The potential falls as \(\dfrac{1}{r}\), unlike the field which falls as \(\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}\), and it is a scalar, so potentials due to several charges add algebraically.

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
stem: Obtain an expression for the de-Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 'V' volts.
solution:
An electron of charge \(e\) and mass \(m\), starting from rest and accelerated through a potential difference of \(V\) volt, gains kinetic energy equal to the work done on it:

\(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = eV\)

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}}\)

Its momentum is therefore

\(p = mv = m\sqrt{\dfrac{2eV}{m}} = \sqrt{2meV}\)

By the de Broglie hypothesis the wavelength associated with a particle of momentum \(p\) is

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\)

\(\therefore \lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}\)

Substituting the numerical values of \(h\), \(m\) and \(e\) gives the convenient working form

\(\lambda = \dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}\)

so an electron accelerated through 100 volt has a wavelength of about \(1.227\ \text{Å}\), comparable with atomic spacings, which is why such electrons are diffracted by crystals.

subtopic: p-n Junction Diode as a Rectifier
stem: With a neat circuit diagram, explain the working of a full wave rectifier. Draw input-output waveforms.
solution:
**Circuit.** The secondary of a centre-tapped transformer feeds two p-n junction diodes \(D_1\) and \(D_2\). The two ends of the secondary go to the p sides of the two diodes, the n sides are joined together, and the load resistance \(R_L\) is connected between that common point and the centre tap of the secondary.

**Working.** The centre tap makes the two halves of the secondary give voltages that are always opposite in sign.

During the **positive half cycle**, the upper end of the secondary is positive, so \(D_1\) is forward biased and conducts while \(D_2\) is reverse biased and does not. Current flows through \(D_1\) and down through \(R_L\).

During the **negative half cycle**, the polarity reverses. Now \(D_2\) is forward biased and conducts while \(D_1\) is cut off. Current flows through \(D_2\), and because of the way the circuit is joined, it passes through \(R_L\) **in the same direction as before**.

So one diode conducts in each half cycle, and the current through the load is unidirectional during both halves. Both halves of the input are used, which is why it is called a full wave rectifier; its output has twice the ripple frequency and roughly twice the average value of a half wave rectifier.

**Waveforms.** The input is a full sine wave. The output consists of the positive humps of the sine wave repeated continuously, with no gaps, since the would-be negative half cycles have been inverted and appear as positive humps too.

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: The string of a guitar is 80 cm long and has a fundamental frequency of 112 Hz. If a guitarist wishes to produce a frequency of 160 Hz, where should he press the string?
solution:
For a stretched string the fundamental frequency is inversely proportional to the vibrating length, the tension and mass per unit length being unchanged:

\(n \propto \dfrac{1}{L}\), so \(n_1 L_1 = n_2 L_2\)

Here \(n_1 = 112\ \text{Hz}\), \(L_1 = 80\ \text{cm}\) and \(n_2 = 160\ \text{Hz}\).

\(112 \times 80 = 160 \times L_2\)

\(L_2 = \dfrac{8960}{160}\)

\(L_2 = 56\ \text{cm}\)

\(\therefore\) the vibrating length must be \(56\ \text{cm}\). The guitarist should press the string at a point \(56\ \text{cm}\) from one end, that is \(24\ \text{cm}\) from the other end.

stem:
0.5 mole of an ideal gas at 300 K, expands isothermally from an initial volume of 2 L to a final volume of 6 L.
Calculate :
(a) work done by the gas
(b) heat supplied to the gas
[ Given : \(R = 8.31\) J mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\) ]
solution:
**(a) Work done by the gas.** For an isothermal expansion of \(n\) moles from volume \(V_1\) to \(V_2\),

\(W = nRT\ln\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = 2.303\,nRT\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\right)\)

Here \(n = 0.5\), \(R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), \(T = 300\ \text{K}\), \(V_1 = 2\ \text{L}\) and \(V_2 = 6\ \text{L}\), so \(\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = 3\).

\(W = 2.303 \times 0.5 \times 8.31 \times 300 \times \log_{10}3\)

\(W = 2.303 \times 1246.5 \times 0.4771\)

\(W = 1369\ \text{J}\)

**(b) Heat supplied to the gas.** The process is isothermal, so the temperature and hence the internal energy of the ideal gas do not change:

\(\Delta U = 0\)

From the first law \(Q = \Delta U + W\),

\(\therefore Q = W = 1369\ \text{J}\)

All the heat supplied is used in doing external work.

stem:
A galvanometer has a resistance of \(40\ \Omega\) and a current of 4 mA is needed for full scale deflection. What is the resistance and how is it to be connected to convert the galvanometer
(a) into an ammeter of 0.4 A range and
(b) into a voltmeter of 5 V range?
solution:
Here \(G = 40\ \Omega\) and \(I_g = 4\ \text{mA} = 4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A}\).

**(a) Ammeter of range 0.4 A.** A **low resistance shunt \(S\) is connected in parallel** with the galvanometer, so that the excess current bypasses the coil. The potential difference across the two is the same:

\(I_g G = (I - I_g)S\)

\(S = \dfrac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{-3} \times 40}{0.4 - 4 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(S = \dfrac{0.16}{0.396}\)

\(S = 0.404\ \Omega\)

**(b) Voltmeter of range 5 V.** A **high resistance \(X\) is connected in series** with the galvanometer, so that the full 5 V is dropped across the combination when the current is \(I_g\):

\(V = I_g(G + X)\)

\(X = \dfrac{V}{I_g} - G = \dfrac{5}{4 \times 10^{-3}} - 40\)

\(X = 1250 - 40\)

\(X = 1210\ \Omega\)

\(\therefore\) a shunt of \(0.404\ \Omega\) in parallel converts it into the ammeter, and a resistance of \(1210\ \Omega\) in series converts it into the voltmeter.

chapter: Magnetic Fields due to Electric Current
stem:
A coaxial cable consists of a central conducting core wire of radius 'a' and a coaxial cylindrical outer conductor of radius 'b'. The two conductors carry equal current in opposite directions, in and out of the plane of the paper. What will be the magnitude of magnetic induction B for (i) \(a < r < b\) and (ii) \(b < r\) ? What will be its direction?
where 'r' is the radius of the Ampere's circular loop.
solution:
Take an Amperian loop in the form of a circle of radius \(r\), concentric with the cable and lying in a plane perpendicular to it. By symmetry \(\vec{B}\) has the same magnitude everywhere on the loop and is tangential to it, so Ampere's law gives

\(\oint\vec{B}\cdot\overrightarrow{dl} = B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enclosed}\)

**(i) For \(a < r < b\)** the loop lies between the two conductors, so it encloses only the current \(I\) of the central core:

\(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\)

\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\)

**Direction:** the lines of induction are circles concentric with the cable, lying in the plane perpendicular to it, with the sense given by the right hand thumb rule applied to the core current.

**(ii) For \(b < r\)** the loop encloses both conductors. They carry equal currents in opposite directions, so

\(I_{enclosed} = I + (-I) = 0\)

\(B(2\pi r) = 0\)

\(\therefore B = 0\) outside the cable, and there is no direction to speak of.

This is the reason a coaxial cable is used to carry signals: its field is entirely confined to the space between the conductors, so it neither radiates nor picks up interference.

stem: Energy of an electron in second Bohr orbit is \(-3.4\) eV. Calculate its kinetic energy and potential energy in third Bohr orbit.
solution:
In a hydrogen atom the energy of the electron in the \(n\)th orbit is

\(E_n = \dfrac{E_1}{n^{2}}\)

From the second orbit, \(E_2 = -3.4\ \text{eV}\), so

\(E_1 = n^{2}E_n = 4 \times (-3.4) = -13.6\ \text{eV}\)

**Total energy in the third orbit:**

\(E_3 = \dfrac{-13.6}{9} = -1.511\ \text{eV}\)

For an electron bound in a Bohr orbit, the kinetic energy is the negative of the total energy and the potential energy is twice the total energy:

**Kinetic energy:**

\(KE = -E_3 = +1.511\ \text{eV}\)

**Potential energy:**

\(PE = 2E_3 = 2 \times (-1.511) = -3.022\ \text{eV}\)

\(\therefore\) in the third orbit the kinetic energy is \(1.511\ \text{eV}\) and the potential energy is \(-3.022\ \text{eV}\). Their sum is \(-1.511\ \text{eV}\), the total energy, as it must be.

stem: Derive Laplace's law for spherical membrane of bubble due to surface tension.
solution:
**Laplace's law for a spherical membrane.** Consider a soap bubble of radius \(r\), made of a liquid of surface tension \(T\). A bubble has a thin film of liquid, so it has **two** free surfaces, an outer and an inner one.

Because of surface tension the film tends to contract, and the pressure inside must exceed that outside for the bubble to be in equilibrium. Let the excess pressure be

\(p = p_{in} - p_{out}\)

Suppose the bubble is blown out slightly, so that its radius increases from \(r\) to \(r + dr\), with \(dr\) very small.

**Work done by the excess pressure.** The force it exerts on the surface is \(p \times 4\pi r^{2}\), and this acts through \(dr\):

\(dW = p \times 4\pi r^{2}\,dr\)   ... (1)

**Increase in surface energy.** The area of one surface increases from \(4\pi r^{2}\) to \(4\pi(r + dr)^{2}\), an increase of \(8\pi r\,dr\) when \(dr^{2}\) is neglected. There are two surfaces, so the total increase in area is \(16\pi r\,dr\), and

\(dW = T \times 16\pi r\,dr\)   ... (2)

The work done by the excess pressure appears as the increase in surface energy, so equating (1) and (2),

\(p \times 4\pi r^{2}\,dr = 16\pi r T\,dr\)

\(\therefore p = \dfrac{4T}{r}\)

This is Laplace's law for a spherical membrane. For a liquid **drop**, which has only one surface, the same argument gives \(p = \dfrac{2T}{r}\). In both cases the excess pressure is greater for a smaller bubble, which is why a small bubble blows itself into a larger one when the two are joined.

stem:
Obtain an expression for maximum safety speed with which a vehicle should move along a curved horizontal road.
Moment of intertia of a solid sphere about its diameter is \(25\ \text{kg m}^{2}\). Calculate its moment of inertia about a tangent.
solution:
**Maximum safety speed on a curved horizontal road.**

Consider a vehicle of mass \(m\) moving on a level circular road of radius \(r\). The road is horizontal, so the normal reaction balances the weight:

\(N = mg\)

The centripetal force needed to keep the vehicle on the curve can come only from the force of static friction between the tyres and the road:

\(f_s = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}\)

Friction cannot exceed its limiting value \(\mu_s N = \mu_s mg\), so the greatest possible speed is reached when friction is at that limit:

\(\dfrac{mv_{\max}^{2}}{r} = \mu_s mg\)

\(\therefore v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s r g}\)

The mass cancels, so the safe speed is the same for a loaded and an empty vehicle, and it falls as the road becomes slippery.

**Moment of inertia of the solid sphere about a tangent.**

About its diameter, \(I_d = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^{2} = 25\ \text{kg m}^{2}\), so

\(MR^{2} = \dfrac{5 \times 25}{2} = 62.5\ \text{kg m}^{2}\)

A tangent is parallel to a diameter and a distance \(R\) from it, so by the theorem of parallel axes

\(I_t = I_d + MR^{2} = 25 + 62.5\)

\(I_t = 87.5\ \text{kg m}^{2}\)

\(\therefore\) the moment of inertia about a tangent is \(87.5\ \text{kg m}^{2}\), which is \(\dfrac{7}{5}MR^{2}\) as expected.

chapter: Kinetic Theory of Gases and Radiation
subtopic: Absorption, Reflection and Transmission of Heat Radiation
stem:
Derive the relation between coefficient of absorption, coefficient of reflection and coefficient of transmission.
Compare the r.m.s. speed of hydrogen molecule at 127°C with r.m.s. speed of oxygen molecule at 27°C, given that molecular masses of hydrogen and oxygen are 2 and 32 respectively.
solution:
**Relation between the coefficients.**

When radiant heat of quantity \(Q\) falls on a body, part of it \(Q_a\) is absorbed, part \(Q_r\) is reflected and the rest \(Q_t\) is transmitted through it. Since energy is conserved,

\(Q = Q_a + Q_r + Q_t\)

Dividing throughout by \(Q\),

\(\dfrac{Q_a}{Q} + \dfrac{Q_r}{Q} + \dfrac{Q_t}{Q} = 1\)

The three fractions are by definition the coefficient of absorption \(a\), the coefficient of reflection \(r\) and the coefficient of transmission \(t\).

\(\therefore a + r + t = 1\)

Each coefficient is a pure number lying between 0 and 1. For a perfectly black body \(a = 1\) and \(r = t = 0\); for an athermanous body \(t = 0\), so \(a + r = 1\).

**Comparison of the r.m.s. speeds.**

The r.m.s. speed of a gas molecule is

\(v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}\), so \(v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{M}}\)

For hydrogen at \(127^{\circ}\text{C} = 400\ \text{K}\) with \(M = 2\), and oxygen at \(27^{\circ}\text{C} = 300\ \text{K}\) with \(M = 32\),

\(\dfrac{v_H}{v_O} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_H/M_H}{T_O/M_O}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{400/2}{300/32}}\)

\(= \sqrt{\dfrac{200}{9.375}} = \sqrt{21.33}\)

\(\dfrac{v_H}{v_O} = 4.62\)

\(\therefore\) the r.m.s. speed of hydrogen at \(127^{\circ}\text{C}\) is about \(4.62\) times that of oxygen at \(27^{\circ}\text{C}\).

subtopic: Self-Inductance and Energy in a Magnetic Field
stem:
Define :
(i) Self inductance
(ii) Mutual inductance
A conducting loop of area \(1\text{m}^{2}\) is placed normal to a uniform magnetic field of \(3\ \text{Wb/m}^{2}\). If the magnetic field is uniformly reduced to \(1\ \text{Wb/m}^{2}\) in 0.5 second, calculate the induced e.m.f. produced in the coil.
solution:
**(i) Self inductance.** The self inductance of a coil is the property by virtue of which it opposes any change of current through itself, by inducing a back e.m.f. Numerically it is the magnetic flux linked with the coil per unit current through it:

\(L = \dfrac{N\phi}{I}\), equivalently \(e = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\)

A coil has self inductance of one henry if a current changing at one ampere per second induces in it a back e.m.f. of one volt.

**(ii) Mutual inductance.** The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the property by virtue of which a change of current in one coil induces an e.m.f. in the other. Numerically it is the flux linked with the secondary per unit current in the primary:

\(M = \dfrac{N_s\phi_s}{I_p}\), equivalently \(e_s = -M\dfrac{dI_p}{dt}\)

Two coils have mutual inductance of one henry if a current in the primary changing at one ampere per second induces an e.m.f. of one volt in the secondary.

**Induced e.m.f. in the loop.** The loop is normal to the field, so the flux through it is \(\phi = BA\) and

\(e = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = -A\dfrac{dB}{dt}\)

Here \(A = 1\ \text{m}^{2}\), the field falls from \(3\ \text{Wb/m}^{2}\) to \(1\ \text{Wb/m}^{2}\) in \(0.5\ \text{s}\),

\(|e| = 1 \times \dfrac{3 - 1}{0.5}\)

\(|e| = 4\ \text{V}\)

\(\therefore\) the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is \(4\ \text{V}\), and by Lenz's law it drives a current that tries to maintain the decreasing flux.

subtopic: Interference and Young's Double Slit Experiment
stem: Using analytical method, obtain an expression for the fringe width of two interfering waves.
solution:
Let two coherent sources \(S_1\) and \(S_2\), a distance \(d\) apart, send light of wavelength \(\lambda\) to a screen a distance \(D\) away, with \(D \gg d\). Take O as the point on the screen equidistant from the sources, and P a point at distance \(y\) from O.

**Path difference.** From the geometry,

\(S_2P^{2} = D^{2} + \left(y + \dfrac{d}{2}\right)^{2}\) and \(S_1P^{2} = D^{2} + \left(y - \dfrac{d}{2}\right)^{2}\)

Subtracting,

\(S_2P^{2} - S_1P^{2} = 2yd\)

\((S_2P + S_1P)(S_2P - S_1P) = 2yd\)

Since \(D \gg d\) and \(D \gg y\), both distances are very nearly \(D\), so \(S_2P + S_1P \approx 2D\). Hence the path difference is

\(\Delta = S_2P - S_1P = \dfrac{yd}{D}\)

**Positions of the bright bands.** A bright band occurs where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, \(\Delta = n\lambda\):

\(\dfrac{y_n d}{D} = n\lambda\), so \(y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

**Fringe width.** The fringe width \(W\) is the distance between two consecutive bright bands:

\(W = y_{n+1} - y_n = \dfrac{(n+1)\lambda D}{d} - \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

\(\therefore W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}\)

The same expression is obtained for consecutive dark bands, so bright and dark fringes are equally spaced. The fringe width does not depend on the order \(n\), which is why the pattern is uniform, and it increases if the screen is moved farther away or the sources are brought closer together.
